blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a study from Li et al. that investigates the growing threat of malvertising—malicious activities exploiting web advertisements. The authors crawled 90,000 top websites and found over 1% had been compromised to deliver malicious content or fraudulent clicks, with large ad networks like DoubleClick infiltrated. The paper details how malvertising works, including a real-world campaign that infected high-traffic sites via a fake AV scam, using cloaking and evasion techniques to evade detection. The study categorizes malvertising attacks into drive-by-downloads, scams/phishing, and click-fraud, revealing that attackers exploit ad networks, redirectors, and compromised publishers. The authors propose detection methods based on identifying malicious nodes in ad-delivery paths, noting that malvertising paths are longer, involve unknown nodes, and use transient domains. Key insights include the rampancy of malvertising, the sophistication of attackers in evading detection, and the vulnerability of smaller ad networks.
paper_title: Knowing your enemy: understanding and detecting malicious web advertising
paper_abstract: 1. Online advertising drives the economy of the World Wide Web. Modern websites of any size and popularity include advertisements to monetize visits from their users. To this end, they assign an area of their web page to an advertising company (so called ad exchange) that will use it to display promotional content. By doing this, the website owner implicitly trusts that the advertising company will offer legitimate content and it will not put the site’s visitors at risk of falling victims of malware campaigns and other scams. In this paper, we perform the first large-scale study of the safety of the advertisements that are encountered by the users on the Web. In particular, we analyze to what extent users are exposed to malicious content through advertisements, and investigate what are the sources of this malicious content. Additionally, we show that some ad exchanges are more prone to serving malicious advertisements than others, probably due to their deficient filtering mechanisms. The observations that we make in this paper shed light on a little studied, yet important, aspect of advertisement networks, and can help both advertisement networks and website owners in securing their web pages and in keeping their visitors safe. The online advertising industry is constantly growing. A recent report showed that this industry generated a revenue of 42.8 billion dollars in 2013, which is 17% higher than what had been reported in the previous year [14]. In the World Wide Web, where most online services are free of charge, advertisements constitute the main revenue for website administrators, and it is very common to see promotional content alongside the actual information contained in such sites. Given the profitability of online advertising, many big players have entered the arena.
